passage:
It happened during the Losar holidays last winter, when I was eleven. I'm Dolma. In an online building game, a player called StarFox kept helping me. After three days, StarFox asked which school I went to and wanted a photo "to see my teammate". Then: "Don't tell your parents, they won't understand."
My stomach went strange. My friend Hafsa had once told me that grown-ups who ask kids for secrets online are a red flag.
I went straight to Amala in the kitchen and showed her the chat. She hugged me, said, "You did exactly right, my girl," and helped me block and report StarFox that same evening. Then we changed my name in the game.
I still play, but I never share where I live or what I look like.

qa.q: What did StarFox want to see?
qa.a: StarFox wanted a photo "to see my teammate".

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when StarFox asked for secrecy?
qa.a: Dolma felt uneasy and scared, with a strange feeling in the stomach, sensing something was wrong.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Amala straight away worked, because a trusted adult helped block and report the contact the same evening and nothing personal was shared.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel if she learned her warning helped?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel glad and proud that what she shared helped her friend stay safe. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details online and telling a trusted adult about a pressuring contact the same day.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
The monsoon had knocked the internet down to one slow bar, and Uma's project on how bats find food was due the next morning.
She typed "how do bats see in the dark". The first result, in bold, said: "Bats are blind! Try our Night Vision Glasses, 50% off!"
"Done," said her cousin Simran, peering over her shoulder. "Bats are blind."
Uma squinted at a tiny word at the top: "Sponsored." "It's an advert. They want to sell glasses."
She waited for the slow pages and opened a museum's page and a school science site. Both said bats can see, and many also use echoes to find insects.
"So the first answer was wrong?" Simran asked.
"Not totally. Just selling something." Uma wrote both sources at the bottom of her chart.

qa.q: What tiny word did Uma notice at the top of the first result?
qa.a: She noticed the word "Sponsored."

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she squinted at the first result?
qa.a: She felt suspicious and unsure, sensing the bold claim was an advert rather than a fact.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend doing online research like Uma?
qa.a: Check whether a result is sponsored, compare at least two trusted sources such as a museum or school site, and write down where the facts came from.

qa.q: How does Simran's view change during the search?
qa.a: Simran first accepts the top answer, then is surprised to learn it was selling something and wasn't fully true.

grounding: Shows a child noticing sponsored content and checking better sources despite slow internet and a deadline.

passage:
On the second night of the Christmas holidays, Thomas, ten, was still gaming at midnight in his Bengaluru flat, headphones on. The next morning he slept through breakfast and snapped at his mother. By afternoon his eyes felt gritty.
His friend Gurleen rang the bell at four. "Cricket in the park? We need one more."
"I'm on level twelve," Thomas said. Then he looked out at the sun and the other kids. He saved the game.
He played till dark and came home starving, cheeks red.
That night he told his mother, "Maybe one hour of games after homework, and the tablet sleeps in the hall." She smiled. "Your idea. I like it."
He was asleep by ten.

qa.q: Where does the tablet sleep in Thomas's new plan?
qa.a: The tablet sleeps in the hall.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling the morning after gaming till midnight?
qa.a: He felt tired and irritable, sleeping through breakfast and snapping at his mother.

qa.q: What small step helped Thomas balance screens with play and sleep?
qa.a: Saying yes to cricket, then suggesting his own one-hour limit with the tablet kept out of his room.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when Thomas comes to play?
qa.a: Gurleen would probably feel happy and relieved, since they needed one more player and Thomas joined in.

grounding: Shows a child noticing how late gaming affects him and choosing a better balance with outdoor play and sleep.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
I'm Kiran, Farida's older brother. During the Eid holidays she spent ages talking to the voice assistant on Ammi's phone.
"Are you my friend?" she asked it.
"I'm here to help!" it said.
"Do you love me?"
"I'm a computer program, so I don't have feelings."
Farida frowned. Then she asked it when Eid was this year, and it said the wrong date, the one from last year. She burst out laughing. "It doesn't even know Eid!"
I told her it's just a program that follows patterns and can make mistakes. She thought about it and said, "So it's like a talking calculator." I don't know if she was disappointed, but later she went to find Nani to ask for a story instead.

qa.q: What date did the voice assistant give for Eid?
qa.a: It gave the wrong date, the one from last year.

qa.q: What might Farida have been feeling when the assistant said it had no feelings?
qa.a: She might have felt a little disappointed or puzzled, since she had hoped it could be her friend.

qa.q: How could Kiran help Farida use voice assistants wisely?
qa.a: He could remind her to check important answers with a person or a trusted source, and that friendship and stories come from real people like Nani.

qa.q: What is it like for Nani when Farida comes to ask for a story?
qa.a: Nani would probably feel pleased and loved, getting quality time with her granddaughter instead of the phone.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a voice assistant is a program that can be wrong and does not truly feel.

passage:
It was the week before Halloween in Toronto, and Rafael had spent an hour carving a pumpkin for the school display. On the way in, Xin bumped it with his backpack. The pumpkin rolled off the steps and cracked.
"Oops," Xin said, grinning.
Rafael's hands balled into fists. He stepped forward. Then he stopped, took a long breath of the cold air, and counted to five like his coach had taught him.
"That took me an hour," he said, his voice shaking. "You need to say sorry."
Xin's grin faded. "It was kind of an accident. Sorry."
His cousin Ana, watching from the door, whispered, "I thought you were going to punch him."
"I wanted to," Rafael admitted.

qa.q: How long had Rafael spent carving the pumpkin?
qa.a: He had spent an hour carving it.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when his hands balled into fists?
qa.a: He felt furious and hurt, because Xin had broken the pumpkin and seemed to find it funny.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pausing to breathe and count, then using clear words, worked because it gave Xin a chance to apologise instead of starting a fight.

qa.q: Why might Ana have expected Rafael to punch Xin?
qa.a: Ana saw his fists and how angry he looked, so she was surprised and relieved that he chose words instead.

grounding: Shows a child pausing before retaliating and choosing words when provoked.

passage:
The winter fog was so thick the school bus crawled, and Yusuf's music recital started in twenty minutes. He had the flute solo.
His hands were cold and shaking. His heart was thumping. "What if I forget the middle part?" he whispered.
His friend Tushar, sitting beside him, said, "Do your thing. The counting thing."
Yusuf closed his eyes. Breathe in for four, hold for four, out for four. He pressed his fingers along the flute in his lap, playing the tune silently from start to end.
The bus arrived with five minutes to spare. On stage, his first note wobbled. He took one slow breath and kept going.
Afterwards, Tushar punched his arm gently. "The middle part was the best bit."

qa.q: How many minutes did the bus have to spare when it arrived?
qa.a: The bus arrived with five minutes to spare.

qa.q: What might Yusuf be worried about on the bus?
qa.a: He was nervous and afraid he would forget the middle part of his flute solo.

qa.q: What calming routine could Yusuf use again before a performance?
qa.a: He could repeat the breathing for four counts and play the tune silently with his fingers, which steadied him even when the bus was late.

qa.q: How does Tushar help Yusuf feel more confident?
qa.a: Tushar reminds him of his calming routine and cheers him after, so Yusuf feels supported and less alone with his nerves.

grounding: Shows a child noticing performance nerves and using a calming routine despite a late, foggy bus ride.

passage:
At the Navratri garba in their colony, Usha, ten, was taller than everyone in her group. As she stepped into the circle, Abhinav called out, "Watch out, the lamp post is dancing!" A few kids laughed.
Usha's cheeks burned. For a moment she wanted to leave. Her Mummy had once told her, "Your body is for dancing and running, not for other people's jokes."
She lifted her chin. "Lamp posts help people see," she said, and kept dancing.
Later, her cousin Meera squeezed her hand. "You were the best one."
At home Usha told Mummy what Abhinav said. Mummy listened, hugged her, and said she would ask the garba organiser aunty to remind the kids that jokes about bodies aren't okay. She called her that same evening.

qa.q: What did Abhinav call Usha?
qa.a: He called her "the lamp post".

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when the kids laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her cheeks burning, and for a moment she wanted to leave.

qa.q: How did Mummy support Usha after the garba?
qa.a: Mummy listened and hugged her, then called the garba organiser the same evening to remind the kids that jokes about bodies aren't okay.

qa.q: Why might Abhinav have made the joke, and what could change for him?
qa.a: Abhinav may have wanted to get laughs without thinking how it felt; if an adult explains the hurt, he might learn not to mock people's bodies.

grounding: Shows a child coping with a hurtful comment about her looks while keeping her self-respect and getting adult support.

passage:
During winter sports week, when I was eleven, a group of boys started calling Usha "Slow Coach" every time she ran. I'm Shreya. On the third day they made her carry all the cones alone while they sang it, and some girls in my team laughed.
I didn't laugh. My stomach hurt. Rina nudged me. "Come on, it's just a joke."
"It's not a joke if she's crying," I said.
At lunch I went to Ms Fernandes, the PE teacher, and told her everything. She listened, thanked me, and said it wasn't my fault for telling. That same afternoon she spoke to the boys, made them apologise, and told Usha's parents. She also moved the cone duty to a rota.
Next day Usha sat with me at lunch. We just ate.

qa.q: What did the boys call Usha?
qa.a: They called her "Slow Coach".

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling while the others laughed?
qa.a: Shreya felt upset and uncomfortable, with a stomach ache, knowing the teasing was hurting Usha.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Refusing to laugh and telling the PE teacher at lunch worked, because the teacher acted that same afternoon to stop the bullying.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Shreya sat with her the next day?
qa.a: Usha probably felt safer and less alone, knowing someone had stood up for her. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child recognising bullying, refusing to join in, and telling a teacher who acts the same day.

passage:
In the monsoon, the drain behind the hostel dining hall became a rushing stream. After dinner, Gargi, Tarun's closest friend, pointed at it. "I dare you to jump across. Everyone's watching."
Tarun looked at the brown, fast water and felt his legs go weak. "No way. That's how people get swept off."
"Scaredy cat," someone said.
"Maybe. Still no." Tarun smiled at Gargi. "Race you to the common room instead? Loser does my laundry."
Gargi laughed and ran. On the way, Tarun stopped at the warden's office. "People are daring each other to jump the drain," he said. The warden went out at once, sent everyone inside, and put a rope and a sign across the path that night.
Gargi rolled her eyes. "Snitch." But she saved him a seat.

qa.q: What did the warden put across the path?
qa.a: The warden put a rope and a sign across the path that night.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he looked at the water?
qa.a: Tarun felt scared, his legs going weak, and sure the dare was dangerous.

qa.q: How did Tarun say no without losing his friend?
qa.a: He refused clearly but kindly, offered a fun race instead, and still told the warden quietly so no one got hurt.

qa.q: How does Gargi seem to feel about Tarun's choice?
qa.a: Gargi teases him as a snitch, but saving him a seat shows she isn't really angry and the friendship is fine.

grounding: Shows a child refusing a risky dare, reporting it to an adult who acts the same night, and keeping the friendship.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage:
Two weeks before Ganesh Chaturthi, Ms Kapoor's class had to build a clay eco-Ganesha model in groups. Bhavna, eleven, took charge of her group. She made a list: Rohan to collect clay, Priya to paint, Nazia to write the card.
Nazia hardly spoke, but she stayed back every day and quietly fixed the cracks in the trunk with wet clay. Without her, it would have fallen apart.
When Ms Kapoor praised the model and turned to Bhavna, saying, "Great leadership!", Bhavna felt proud. But she said, "Thank you, Miss. Nazia saved it, though. She fixed all the cracks."
Nazia looked up, surprised, and turned pink.
Rohan whispered, "I didn't even notice." After that, he asked Nazia to help with the next project.

qa.q: What was Nazia's job on Bhavna's list?
qa.a: Nazia was to write the card.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Bhavna gave her credit?
qa.a: Nazia felt surprised and a little shy, turning pink, but probably also proud that her quiet work was noticed. 😊

qa.q: What makes Bhavna's leadership fair in this story?
qa.a: She organised clear jobs, and when praised she shared credit with the person who did the key hidden work.

qa.q: How does Rohan's view of Nazia change?
qa.a: Rohan hadn't noticed her work before, but after hearing about it he respects her enough to ask for her help next time.

grounding: Shows a child leading a group task and giving fair credit to a quiet contributor.
